digests.narrative: His conviction in this theme is at its highest and the tape moved hardest against it. Sivers' quarter is the centrepiece: an opportunity pipeline of $1.2bn, up 268% since December, six new pluggable players with three in alpha sample evaluation, Jabil initial production orders guided to H1 2027 with the ramp in H2, and a new foundry partner whose capacity he stresses is available now, de-risking the single-source dependence on Win Semi. He reads the CW laser shortage as structural because Lumentum and Coherent have allocated too much capacity to NVIDIA to serve the merchant market, and Coherent has said it will not sell indium phosphide lasers externally at all. Semtech corroborated from another angle, reporting that availability now matters more than pricing, no erosion on booked optical orders, 1.6T FiberEdge qualifications finishing early and over 70% of next year already booked. Against that he turned critical on his own largest position, writing that Applied Optoelectronics is getting harder to support through repeated $500m and $600m ATMs and that the share structure is becoming shareholder unfriendly. He also judges MACOM and AOI likely absent from first-generation CPO deployments, a smaller pool Sivers sits inside. He called the sector's underperformance absurd on 20 August given demand visibility; it then got materially worse.
keyPoints: Sivers pipeline $1.2bn, up 268% since December, with six new pluggable engagements and a second foundry
Jabil initial production orders dated H1 2027, ramp H2 2027 — the first hard date in the theme
CW laser shortage structural because Lumentum and Coherent allocate to NVIDIA and Coherent will not sell InP externally
He turned on AOI's ATMs: shareholder-unfriendly financing even with the operating outlook intact
He judges MACOM and AOI likely out of first-generation CPO; Sivers inside it
Demand visibility repeatedly described as three to five years, against revenue that is still pre-ramp

digests.narrative: He remains structurally bullish and has rotated within the theme rather than out of it. His position through H1 2026 was heavily overweight memory across Micron, SanDisk, Phison, Silicon Motion, Nanya, Macronix, Winbond and the Korean names, and he has since trimmed everything except the Samsung and SK Hynix exposure on the view that the largest price-discovery period has already played out — Micron having gone from $300 to above $1,000 — leaving a waiting game for operating income to catch up. NVIDIA's quarter then validated the underlying shortage from the buyer's side, with commitments tripling on memory procurement and management describing extreme pricing conditions. The newer idea is a cascade further down the stack into legacy DDR2 and DDR3, where he sees price hikes reaching 40-60% quarter on quarter as Winbond withdraws from certain lines, and he has taken positions in Taiwanese names on that basis, describing it as another SanDisk-style earnings inflection. On SanDisk itself he points to investor-day figures of roughly 80% adjusted gross margin and about $93bn of minimum contracted revenue, with long-term agreements covering two thirds of 2028 output, which he argues makes it hard to call cyclical.
keyPoints: Structurally bullish but trimmed after the re-rating; holds Samsung and SK Hynix exposure
NVIDIA's tripled commitments and extreme-pricing comment validate the shortage from the buyer's side
New cascade into legacy DDR2/DDR3 with 40-60% quarterly hikes as Winbond exits lines
SanDisk: ~80% adjusted gross margin target and ~$93bn minimum contracted revenue
US pressure on Apple over Chinese memory hands pricing power back to the non-Chinese suppliers

digests.narrative: His attention here is on the photonics transition rather than on leading-edge logic. GlobalFoundries is the active idea: he argues the US government taking a material stake alongside a CHIPS Act award should re-accelerate revenue as CPO scales, and expressed surprise the stock was down given a direct government stake advancing the technology, reading it as unrewarded good news. His emphasis in those posts is usually the read-through to the laser suppliers qualifying into the platform rather than a standalone case for the foundry. TSMC he names as sitting at the centre of the AI buildout and as the source on memory and ABF substrate tightness over the next several years, but he rarely argues it directly. Tower appears in the silicon-photonics foundry-capacity discussion and through its InP epiwafer agreements securing strategic III-V supply, which he cites mainly as evidence of demand for IQE. Intel appears only as a factual relay — a process timeline pulled forward, the government stake as historical precedent — with no directional case attached in any recent post.
keyPoints: GlobalFoundries: government stake plus CPO framed as unrewarded good news
His GFS posts usually route the conclusion to the laser suppliers qualifying into the platform
TSMC named as central to the buildout and as the source on ABF substrate tightness, but rarely argued
Tower's InP epiwafer agreements cited as evidence of III-V demand rather than as a Tower case
Intel relayed factually with no directional view in any recent post

digests.narrative:
He treats neocloud demand as settled and argues the read-through is enormous. CoreWeave's backlog above $104B, excluding more than $25B of new customer agreements added in early Q3, is his headline evidence, and he explicitly extends it to Nebius and IREN. Supermicro guiding $65-72B of revenue is cited alongside it as the same signal from the hardware side.

Nebius is the name he follows most closely. He called the last outlook insane again — $582.3M of revenue, up 454% year on year and 46% sequentially, at roughly 50% adjusted EBITDA margin in AI Cloud, with $8.04B of cash — while noting honestly that he had hoped for a guidance raise and only got a reiteration of $3.0-3.4B for 2026 and $7-9B exit ARR. He has also used the hyperscaler prints as a sarcastic argument against shorting it.

On the colocation side he flagged Riot's $9.1B twenty-year agreement, extendable to $16.1B, alongside AMD exercising its expansion option, and placed most of the basket's revenue inflection in the second half of 2027 — Riot's first 96MW targeted for December 2027. He grouped Nebius with the laser names as one of the places where 2027 demand visibility is unusually good.
keyPoints: CoreWeave's $104B+ backlog, excluding $25B+ added in early Q3, read across to NBIS and IREN
NBIS Q2: $582.3M revenue +454% Y/Y at ~50% adjusted EBITDA margin, $8.04B cash
Noted the guidance was reiterated, not raised — $3.0-3.4B revenue, $7-9B exit ARR
RIOT's $9.1B/20-year deal extendable to $16.1B, with AMD expanding separately
Colocation revenue inflections concentrated in H2 2027

digests.narrative:
Substrates are where he thinks the shortage is most visible and least priced. He posted the indium phosphide story as the clearest evidence yet: prices began rising in Q4 last year and the latest increase is the fourth consecutive one, expected to exceed 10%, while epitaxial wafer prices made from those substrates have already risen twice and are heading for a third increase. His favourite detail is a supplier saying that even if you have the money, you still may not be able to get the material.

He claims the call — he predicted the squeeze last year — and holds both AXT and IQE, saying his February IQE thesis was validated alongside AXT and that he remains long both. He notes the reporting is Taiwan-centric and names VPEC, Landmark and IET as beneficiaries, and treats MACOM's long-term epiwafer agreements and equity stake in IQE as a soft backstop that reads positive for IQE specifically.

On packaging he holds Amkor as a duration bet rather than a momentum one — bought on post-earnings weakness he found surprising given the Nvidia deal and a ten-year TSMC agreement, and explicitly described as more of a 2028 name with a separate 2027 ramp. Applied Materials raising advanced packaging growth guidance and extending customer discussions to 2030 supports the direction.
keyPoints: InP substrate prices up for a fourth consecutive quarter, the latest hike expected above 10%
Epitaxial wafer prices already raised twice, moving toward a third increase
Suppliers reportedly telling customers that money alone will not secure material
He is long both AXT and IQE and says he called the squeeze a year early
The cited reporting credits Taiwanese players VPEC, Landmark and IET as beneficiaries
Amkor held as a 2028 duration bet backstopped by Nvidia and a ten-year TSMC agreement

digests.narrative: Marvell is the active name. He reads the Google warrant arrangement as spanning TPU compute, storage and networking, and frames NVIDIA as having watched Marvell network its way into every hyperscaler, citing a $12.2bn option against roughly $120bn of revenue opportunity. He also expects Marvell to benefit most from the Maia 300 ramp, pointing to more than 300k units in 2027 with expansion beyond a million, and notes it now owns Celestial, which places it inside the optical interposer layer — the same move he believes squeezed POET out. Semtech he covers through its quarter rather than a valuation view, highlighting that availability matters more than pricing, that CW laser revenue for transceivers begins in the first half of fiscal 2028 with capacity explicitly limited, and that management targets above 50% market share in 1.6T FiberEdge by year end while saying current capacity may not be enough for fiscal 2028. Broadcom appears mainly as a valuation comparator among the Western CPO leaders and as one of the remaining Western CW laser players. Nokia is named only as a party evaluating X-FAB's photonics foundry.
keyPoints: Marvell: Google warrant deal across TPU compute, storage and networking, $12.2bn option
Marvell expected to benefit most from the Maia 300 ramp, 300k+ units in 2027
Owning Celestial puts Marvell in the interposer layer he thinks squeezed POET out
Semtech targets 50%+ share in 1.6T FiberEdge; CW transceiver revenue starts H1 FY28
Broadcom used as a valuation comparator; Nokia only an X-FAB evaluation partner

digests.narrative:
This card changes shape this week: LPKF moves into the glass layer from materials, so the theme finally contains the name through which glass-substrate progress actually reaches the book. It is still only two tickers.

The news is a delay, and it is the analyst reporting a setback in his own theme, which is the kind of disclosure worth weighting heavily. Samsung Electro-Mechanics has delayed its semiconductor glass substrate investment on a bottleneck in customer reliability evaluations of prototypes, revising the start of operations to 2028, with SKC also pushing back. For an equipment supplier this is worse than it is for a substrate maker: the tool order lands before the line runs, so a customer moving its start date right moves LPKF's revenue with it, and there is no partial credit. The share price is down about 12% on the month, which is the market reading the same thing.

Corning remains the other half of the card and has not moved: its glass-bridge case rests on 2028 fibre array unit TAM rather than anything shipping, and co-packaged optics delay reports weigh on that and the FAU case together. Conviction stays low. Glass is a 2028-2029 layer on current evidence, and the datapoint that would change this card is a disclosed tool order from a named substrate customer with a delivery year attached — not another timeline article.
keyPoints: LPK.DE re-categorised into glass from materials — the layer now holds the equipment exposure directly
Samsung Electro-Mechanics delays glass substrate start of operations to 2028; SKC also pushes back
Equipment leads the line, so a customer's slip moves LPKF's revenue event with it
LPK.DE is down about 12% on the month against a flat tape
GLW's glass-bridge case still rests on 2028 FAU TAM rather than current shipments
What would change the card: a disclosed LIDE order from a named customer with a delivery year

digests.narrative: He treats humanoids as the next major theme after space and AI, and is explicit that he wants downstream leaders rather than component suppliers. He is personally trying to own as much of Agility Robotics as possible, arguing that its application-specific approach — already deployed in Amazon and Mercado Libre warehouses — is further along in commercialization than the general-purpose programmes, and that its robots do not need to do backflips to do packaging and delivery work. He uses the Chinese listings as the valuation argument: Unitree's public listing at a far larger market capitalisation shows demand for pure-play humanoids is bigger than public markets expected, and XPeng carving out its robotics unit at a $6.3bn-plus valuation points the same way. On Tesla he is directly sceptical, writing that Optimus is wrapped inside a trillion-dollar company so it is not the pure-play exposure he is pointing at, and separately that he does not think Tesla can pull off general purpose yet. On upstream suppliers he is deliberately absent: mass production numbers are still too small, so he is not allocating much to actuator and component names, and tempers even the more focused ones on scale grounds.
keyPoints: Wants downstream humanoid leaders, not upstream component suppliers, until volumes scale
Agility framed as ahead on commercialization via Amazon and Mercado Libre warehouse deployments
Chinese listings — Unitree, XPeng's robotics carve-out — used as the valuation read-across
Explicitly sceptical on Tesla: Optimus is not pure-play exposure and general purpose is unproven
Component suppliers tempered: scale is vastly different until humanoid volumes are massive

digests.narrative: NVIDIA's 26 August print reset the anchor for every downstream estimate. Revenue of $96.22bn beat expectations near $92.17bn, data centre came in at $89.0bn, and the guide was $108bn while assuming zero China data centre compute revenue. He judged the outlook statement more important than the beat: management guided fiscal 2028 revenue growth of roughly 70% against a 43.9% consensus and called it supply constrained, with cloud industry backlog above $2tn and top-five hyperscaler capex framed at nearly $800bn in 2026 and $1.3tn in 2027. Commitments rose from $119bn to $279bn, primarily memory procurement, and the CFO described extreme pricing conditions in memory — which he reads as direct confirmation of his memory positions rather than as a cost problem. His stated conclusion is that with NVIDIA already above $5tn the alpha now comes from how its architecture and capacity decisions land elsewhere in the chain, in CPO, memory and 800V power, rather than from mispricing in NVIDIA itself. On AMD he expects Helios plus CPUs to bring another inflection, helped by copying the neocloud fundraise-to-GPU flywheel, and notes an open question about which partner Helios uses now that AOI looks out of the picture.
keyPoints: Fiscal 2028 revenue growth guided near 70% against 43.9% consensus, explicitly supply constrained
Commitments $119bn to $279bn, largely memory procurement; CFO cites extreme memory pricing
Hyperscaler capex framed at ~$800bn in 2026 rising to $1.3tn in 2027; cloud backlog above $2tn
He argues the alpha is downstream of the print — CPO, memory, 800V — not in NVIDIA itself
AMD: Helios plus CPUs as the next inflection, with the optical partner still unresolved

digests.narrative:
He uses the hyperscalers as the demand proof rather than as positions. His summary of the last earnings round is that Amazon, Meta, Alphabet and Microsoft guided combined 2026 capex to roughly $720-745B, up from $695-725B previously, with Amazon at $220B, Google $195-205B, Meta $130-145B and Microsoft $175B. He raised Amazon's number himself after the quarter, noting it moved to $220B from $200B partly on higher memory costs, which he read as bullish for Micron and Samsung.

His sharper point is the gap between media framing and disclosure. Where the coverage said hyperscalers had overbuilt and were reselling excess compute, he pointed out that all four reported demand exceeding capacity. He quotes Jassy saying Amazon will not have enough capacity to meet all 2026 demand and expects the same in 2027, with most incoming 2027 capacity already reserved and substantial 2028 capacity reserved too. He used the same material as a sarcastic template for how to research a short on Nebius — read the hyperscaler prints first, find record demand and backlog everywhere, then conclude.

The Marvell-Alphabet arrangement is the week's specific item: Marvell granting Alphabet options to buy $12.2B of the company across TPU-related technologies, which he suggests could translate into roughly $120B of revenue through 2033, with separate Amazon warrants following the Celestial acquisition.
keyPoints: 2026 combined capex guided to ~$720-745B, raised from $695-725B
Amazon's $220B guide raised on higher memory costs — read as confirmation for MU and Samsung
All four reported demand exceeding capacity, against media framing of overbuild
Jassy: most 2027 capacity already reserved, with substantial 2028 capacity reserved
MRVL granting GOOGL options on $12.2B of stock across TPU technologies

digests.narrative:
This layer exists because the desk built it, not because the feed produced it. Every thesis that touches power reaches it through a list rather than an argument. Bloom Energy is the only sustained name: it appears in a late-July recap for 166% year-on-year revenue growth with expanding margins and raised 2026 guidance, and again in the note that grid power bottlenecks triggered a five-fold increase, to $25B, in Brookfield's financing for its fuel cells. That financing line is the clearest power-constraint datapoint anywhere in the feed.

The second thread is a components one and sits mostly outside the US listed set: a shortage of high-power cylindrical cells for battery backup units, with Samsung SDI supplying Simplo, which assembles for Meta and Amazon, and both Panasonic and Samsung reported short. Vertiv, Eaton, EnerSys and BorgWarner are named only as adjacent read-throughs, and the analyst says plainly it is outside his domain.

GE Vernova and Constellation carry no analyst mentions at all, which is exactly the tiering caveat this layer was built to expose: grid interconnection, transformers and on-site generation are load-bearing for every gigawatt in the neocloud and hyperscaler digests, and the feed prices none of it. Conviction is low because the evidence is thin, not because the constraint is.
keyPoints: Desk-built layer: no thesis in the feed argues power directly, only in passing
BE is the only sustained name — 166% YoY revenue growth, raised 2026 guidance
Grid power bottlenecks drove a 5x increase, to $25B, in Brookfield's financing for BE fuel cells
A BBU cylindrical-cell shortage runs through Samsung SDI, Panasonic and Murata, with no direct US listing
VRT, ETN and ENS appear only as adjacent read-throughs, explicitly outside the analyst's domain
GEV and CEG carry zero analyst mentions, so they cannot rise above radar however load-bearing they are
